question: Why do transformers trained on in-context n-gram prediction pause at simpler sub-n-gram solutions, and can those plateaus be tied to small gradients of the population cross-entropy rather than inferred only from loss curves?

key_findings.claim: The paper gives a model-independent sufficient condition for population cross-entropy stationarity: a predictor that equals the conditional next-token law on a chosen history statistic is stationary when its score is measurable with respect to that same statistic.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma 3.1 factors the gradient into a prediction residual and score; Proposition 3.2 then makes the residual conditionally mean zero when both the prediction and score depend only on the selected suffix. The appendix proves the statement and extends the conditioning statistic beyond contiguous suffixes.

anchors.section: C Proof of the Stationarity Characterization

key_findings.claim: A hand-specified two-layer attention-only transformer can implement every in-context k-gram empirical estimator for k at most n by activating the first-layer heads that retrieve the relevant k-1 history tokens and zeroing the remaining heads.
key_findings.evidence: The first layer concatenates token streams retrieved at fixed relative offsets; the second layer hard-matches the resulting histories and averages successor one-hots. Equations 8a-8c give the sub-n-gram parameter settings, and Lemma B.1 verifies the construction as the attention scale tends to infinity.

anchors.section: B.1 Representing k-grams with Simplified Transformer

key_findings.claim: At those constructed k-gram solutions, the population gradient becomes small only in a joint long-context, large-attention-scale limit.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 4.1 bounds the gradient norm by a square-root attention-scale factor times the k-gram estimation error plus an exponentially small softmax term. With attention scale proportional to context length, the Markov estimation error and softmax leakage vanish; the proof controls derivatives through the self-bounding property of softmax and the matched-history set.

key_findings.claim: The stationarity argument is not intrinsically limited to contiguous k-gram suffixes, but the broader result requires the model score to discard exactly the same coordinates as the predictor.
key_findings.evidence: The main text notes arbitrary history subsets, and Appendix F.2 constructs noncontiguous activated-head sets. Remark C.2 states the general partition condition, showing that the substance is conditional measurability rather than contiguity.

key_findings.claim: In the principal trigram experiment, Adam training visibly traverses uniform, bigram-like, and trigram-like regimes, and the attention maps agree with that interpretation.
key_findings.evidence: For vocabulary size 5 and context length 32, the test loss has two long plateaus and a later drop. At the intermediate plateau both first-layer heads attend to the previous token; at the end one remains at offset -1 while the other moves to offset -2. Figure 3 was directly inspected and makes the discrete attention change visible.

key_findings.claim: The qualitative sequence survives a more conventional attention-only transformer with residual addition, positional embeddings, and learned or one-hot embeddings, but remains a tiny synthetic trigram result.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix I trains vocabulary-3, length-32 models for 4096 Adam steps and shows, over five seeds, an intermediate regime favoring the contiguous -1 offset before learning the -2 dependency. Adding an MLP changes the route: a single head can form both offsets after a unigram plateau, so the specific head-by-head trajectory is architecture-dependent.

anchors.section: I.2 Contiguous Solutions and I.3 Gradient Norms

key_findings.claim: Measured gradient norms are low on the observed plateaus and spike during transitions, which is consistent with the near-stationary picture but does not identify the escape mechanism.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 6-8 overlay loss and full-gradient norms and show small norms during flat phases with pronounced peaks near loss drops. These are same-run correlations; there is no perturbation, Hessian analysis, stochastic escape law, or prediction of transition time from the theorem.

anchors.section: I.3 Plot of Norms of the Gradients

key_findings.claim: The paper explains why a completed sub-n-gram computation can be sticky, not why SGD reaches it, escapes it, or visits subsolutions in a particular order.
key_findings.evidence: The theorem evaluates gradients at constructed parameter configurations. The conclusion itself calls the analysis static and leaves stochastic optimization between plateaus to future work; the narrative attributing escape to curvature or noise is therefore a hypothesis rather than a derived result.

anchors.section: 4.4 On the Emergence of Syntactic Structure

key_findings.claim: Claims that the proof naturally extends to a general transformer should be read as a construction sketch, not an established full-architecture stationarity theorem.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix F.1 sketches residual addition, positional embeddings, an MLP approximation to logarithms, and a generalized value map. It then explicitly says that proving the relevant gradients vanish for the generalized value matrices requires additional work.

method.core_idea: Turn a conditional-expectation identity for cross-entropy gradients into explicit near-stationary transformer configurations that compute progressively higher-order empirical Markov predictors.
method.mechanism: Orthogonal token embeddings and fixed relative attention maps make separate first-layer heads retrieve history offsets. A second softmax compares concatenated histories and averages tokens following matching occurrences. Deactivating heads yields a k-gram estimator. At such a solution, score derivatives inherit only the selected history, so conditional residual cancellation plus softmax self-bounding makes the population gradient small as context length and attention scale grow.
assumptions: Sequences come from an in-context n-gram process whose transition tensor is redrawn from a prior for each sequence.
The main theorem uses the population loss, not a finite training sample or minibatch objective.
Token embeddings are orthogonal and the simplified architecture disentangles and concatenates head streams.
Relative positions are encoded by freely specified attention matrices rather than learned standard positional parameters in the main proof.
The k-gram estimator is approached as the attention norm c tends to infinity and its statistical error vanishes as context length T tends to infinity.
The score at the constructed solution depends only on the same selected history used by the predictor.
No weight decay, finite-window correction, optimizer-noise model, or transition-time analysis enters the theorem.

techniques.role: Cancels the population cross-entropy gradient by conditioning residuals on the statistic that determines the score.
Assigns one first-layer head to each history offset so head activation directly indexes sub-n-gram order.
Uses large-scale softmax attention to average successors of matching k-1 histories.
Controls derivatives of nearly zero attention weights and suppresses unmatched-history gradient terms.
Converts convergence of empirical k-gram counts into a vanishing asymptotic gradient term.
Interprets plateaus using directly visualized attention offsets and gradient norms.

evaluations.setting: Simplified two-layer transformer on in-context trigram data, vocabulary 5, context 32, Dirichlet concentration 0.5
evaluations.metric: Test cross-entropy and first-layer attention maps over 2^14 Adam updates
evaluations.result: Uniform attention gives way to a bigram plateau with both heads at -1, then a trigram solution with heads at -1 and -2
evaluations.baseline: No competing optimizer or architectural baseline; within-run comparison of successive checkpoints

evaluations.metric: Full gradient norm aligned with test loss
evaluations.result: Gradient norm remains low on plateaus and peaks during the transition
evaluations.baseline: Correlational time trace without curvature, noise, or causal perturbation controls

evaluations.setting: More conventional attention-only transformer, vocabulary 3, context 32, one-hot or learned embeddings, five seeds
evaluations.metric: Loss plateaus and head attention-offset structure
evaluations.result: The contiguous -1 solution is generally learned before the -2 dependency
evaluations.baseline: Embedding variants and seeds; still only synthetic trigrams

evaluations.setting: General transformer variant with an MLP
evaluations.result: Only a unigram plateau is prominent and one head later represents both needed offsets
evaluations.baseline: Attention-only route, demonstrating architecture-dependent developmental paths

limitations: The main result is asymptotic in both sequence length and parameter norm; finite-context behavior is not characterized.
The theorem concerns population loss and constructed configurations, not the empirical objective followed by minibatch Adam.
The analysis is static and does not prove attraction, stability, escape, phase order, or transition timing.
The principal architecture has orthogonal tokens, hand-coded relative attention structure, stream concatenation, and a fixed second-layer value map.
Experiments cover tiny synthetic trigram sources and do not test natural-language corpora or pretrained LMs.
General-transformer extensions are partly sketches; the appendix leaves a value-matrix gradient proof open.
Weight decay, finite windows, transition-kernel misspecification, nonstationarity, and tokenizer effects are absent from the theory.
A low gradient norm along one trajectory does not establish a stationary basin or rule out slow ill-conditioned motion.
failure_modes: At finite context, sparse histories can make empirical k-gram estimates noisy enough that the constructed point is not close to stationary.
Finite attention scale leaks mass to mismatched histories and invalidates hard-match reasoning.
Regularization or shared value/residual pathways can give deactivated heads nonzero gradients.
Correlated or nonorthogonal embeddings can entangle token identity with positional retrieval.
An observed plateau may arise from conditioning, optimizer step size, saturation, or finite-sample noise rather than a sub-n-gram computation.
Different architectures can realize the same statistical order with different head allocations, so offset maps are not universal developmental markers.
A sub-n-gram solution may be near-stationary yet never be visited from realistic initialization.
Noise may escape a plateau in a direction unrelated to increasing grammatical order.
reusable_insights: For cross-entropy, matching the conditional law on a statistic is insufficient for stationarity unless parameter scores are measurable with respect to that statistic too.
Softmax saturation can make an implemented sparse algorithm locally sticky because unused routes also receive tiny derivatives.
Plateau claims should jointly measure behavior, circuit state, gradient norm, curvature, and controlled escape rather than infer mechanism from loss alone.
Constructed subsolutions provide useful intervention targets: initialize at, clamp, destabilize, or transplant them to test whether they causally gate later circuits.
Developmental order can be a property of parameterization and residual pathways, not only of task complexity.
Arbitrary selected-history statistics offer a cleaner test bed than contiguous n-grams for separating syntactic order from positional simplicity.
open_questions: What estimator and gradient scale arise at realistic finite context lengths when higher-order histories are rarely repeated?
Which Hessian directions and optimizer-noise statistics determine whether and when a sub-n-gram solution is escaped?
Does a frozen checkpoint-level certificate predict the next learned history coordinate across seeds, architectures, and task priors?
Can causal clamping of sub-n-gram computations advance or delay later induction-head formation under matched update dose?
How do weight decay, normalization, residual mixing, learned positions, and MLPs alter the stationary set?
Do analogous conditional-score stationary points explain developmental plateaus in natural-language models after controlling for other low-gradient causes?
When several noncontiguous subhistories are equally predictive, what breaks symmetry among them during training?
Can a finite-sample theorem distinguish genuine near-stationarity from slow passage through an ill-conditioned region?

competitive_landscape.title: The Evolution of Statistical Induction Heads: In-Context Learning Markov Chains
competitive_landscape.difference: Edelman et al. document uniform-to-unigram-to-bigram phases and give a limited theoretical account for first-order Markov ICL; this paper supplies a general conditional-score stationarity criterion and explicit sub-k solutions for arbitrary n, but still does not derive escape dynamics.

competitive_landscape.title: How Transformers Learn Causal Structure with Gradient Descent
competitive_landscape.difference: Nichani et al. prove gradient descent learns latent causal edges through mutual-information-shaped gradients, including a Markov induction-head case; this paper instead characterizes gradients at preconstructed sub-n-gram predictors and therefore covers stationary geometry rather than the route to the solution.

competitive_landscape.title: Attention with Markov: A Framework for Principled Analysis of Transformers via Markov Chains
competitive_landscape.difference: Attention with Markov characterizes unigram local minima and bigram global minima for single-layer models under data and architecture regimes; this paper studies two-layer in-context empirical estimators and a broader score-measurability condition for sub-n-gram near-stationarity.

competitive_landscape.title: Transformers on Markov Data: Constant Depth Suffices
competitive_landscape.difference: Rajaraman et al. show a three-layer single-head construction for any-order Markov empirical conditionals and logarithmic-depth attention-only composition; this paper uses order-scaled first-layer heads to expose a nested family of solutions and analyzes their local gradients.

competitive_landscape.title: Transformers Can Represent n-gram Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Svete and Cotterell exactly represent fixed n-gram distributions using hard or sparse attention; the present target represents in-context empirical k-gram estimators with softmax limits and asks whether those parameter states are near-stationary under training loss.

competitive_landscape.title: Unveiling Induction Heads: Provable Training Dynamics and Feature Learning in Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen et al. analyze gradient-flow convergence of copier, selector, and classifier components in a richer two-attention-layer n-gram model; this paper offers a simpler and more general stationary-point lens but no comparable end-to-end convergence theorem.

competitive_landscape.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
competitive_landscape.difference: Olsson et al. causally connect induction heads to ICL in small attention-only models and correlate their emergence with a loss bump at larger scale; this paper isolates a synthetic statistical mechanism for plateau stickiness without testing the broad ICL hypothesis.

competitive_landscape.title: Loss Landscape Degeneracy and Stagewise Development in Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: Hoogland et al. use local learning coefficients to align empirical developmental stages with changes in loss-landscape degeneracy in a small LM; this paper derives explicit near-zero first-order gradients for a tractable Markov task but does not estimate singular geometry in learned language models.

competitive_landscape.title: Task Diversity Shortens the ICL Plateau
competitive_landscape.difference: Kim et al. manipulate joint task diversity and show shorter ICL plateaus, directly probing an optimization intervention; this paper identifies candidate stationary subsolutions but does not predict how data diversity alters their stability or escape time.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Sub-n-gram estimators form near-stationary points of population cross-entropy, providing a loss-landscape explanation for stagewise n-gram learning.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The genuinely new core is the conditional-score sufficient condition combined with explicit all-k transformer constructions and a nonasymptotic gradient bound; experiments visualize matching plateaus and attention offsets.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Novel and useful as a static local-geometry result. It advances beyond reports of unigram/bigram phases and pure representation theorems, but it should not be credited with explaining solution selection, escape, transition order, or natural-language emergence. The general-transformer claim is only partially proved.

reviewer_notes: Every extracted page 1-40 was inspected, including proofs, derivative calculations, extensions, and experimental appendices; Figures 3 and 6 were also rendered and directly checked. The pinned export.arxiv PDF is the current arXiv v2 (last revised 2025-08-19) and is marked ICML 2025. Equation text extraction on Theorem 4.1 is typographically imperfect, so this reading preserves the theorem's two-term structure and asymptotic dependencies without inventing garbled symbols. No contradiction invalidates the main theorem; the material scope tension is between a proved static near-stationarity result and narrative language about why training escapes or why syntactic structures emerge.
